lever: Stabilise residual BUBR1 protein through NAD+/SIRT2 regulation
why: Oral NAD+ precursor that raised NAD+ and, via SIRT2-dependent deacetylation of BUBR1 K668, increased BUBR1 levels and lifespan in BubR1-hypomorphic mice (North et al. 2014), the direct precedent for this lever.
caveat: A dietary supplement rather than an approved drug, with no MVA data; one would first need to show the patient's missense BUBR1 protein is expressed, is destabilised by turnover, and is restored by NAD+ repletion in patient cells before any clinical claim.

lever: Stabilise residual BUBR1 protein through NAD+/SIRT2 regulation
why: Alternative NAD+ precursor entering the salvage pathway downstream of NAMPT, tested in human trials with good tolerability, offering a second route to raise NAD+ for SIRT2-mediated BUBR1 stabilisation.
caveat: Unapproved supplement with contested cellular uptake and no evidence of effect on BUBR1 in humans; patient-cell pharmacodynamics (NAD+ rise plus BUBR1 protein increase) would have to be demonstrated.

lever: Stabilise residual BUBR1 protein through NAD+/SIRT2 regulation
why: FDA-approved since 1982 and the best-characterised prescription NAD+ precursor, with proven ability to raise tissue NAD+ (as shown in mitochondrial myopathy trials).
caveat: Flushing, hepatotoxicity at sustained-release doses and lipid effects complicate chronic paediatric use, and no link between niacin dosing and BUBR1 abundance has been shown.

lever: Stabilise residual BUBR1 protein through NAD+/SIRT2 regulation
why: Widely available, approved/GRAS vitamin B3 form used chronically at gram doses (e.g. in dermatology) that efficiently replenishes NAD+ through the salvage pathway.
caveat: Nicotinamide is itself a product-inhibitor of sirtuins including SIRT2, so it could counteract the very deacetylation step this lever depends on; the net effect on BUBR1 acetylation and stability would need direct measurement.

lever: Stabilise residual BUBR1 protein through NAD+/SIRT2 regulation
why: Approved (outside the US) nicotinic acid analogue with far less flushing, used in trials as a tolerable means of modulating NAD+/mitochondrial metabolism.
caveat: Its capacity to raise intracellular NAD+ is much weaker evidenced than NR or niacin and no BUBR1 data exist, so target engagement would have to be established first.

lever: Read through the premature stop codon
why: Oral 80S-ribosome modulator approved in the EU for nonsense-mutation Duchenne muscular dystrophy, the prototype agent for promoting readthrough of premature stop codons such as a BUB1B stop-gained allele.
caveat: Readthrough at the specific BUB1B codon/context is untested and ataluren's own efficacy has been inconsistent in trials, so cell-based evidence of restored full-length BUB1B protein and corrected mitotic checkpoint/aneuploidy readouts would be required first.

lever: Read through the premature stop codon
why: Aminoglycoside that mispairs at premature termination codons and has produced measurable readthrough and partial protein restoration in several nonsense-mutation diseases, and is widely approved as an antibiotic.
caveat: Nephrotoxicity and irreversible ototoxicity make chronic systemic use in a child essentially prohibitive, and readthrough levels are usually low and variant-dependent, so patient-cell dosing/response data would be needed.

lever: Read through the premature stop codon
why: Another approved aminoglycoside with documented premature-stop-codon readthrough activity and somewhat different toxicity kinetics than gentamicin.
caveat: Same ototoxic/nephrotoxic ceiling and unproven readthrough at this codon; any use would need ex vivo demonstration of BUB1B protein recovery plus audiologic and renal monitoring.

lever: Read through the premature stop codon
why: A designed eukaryotic ribosome-selective glycoside built for readthrough with reduced oto/nephrotoxicity, tested clinically in nonsense-mutation cystic fibrosis and cystinosis.
caveat: Investigational only (no approval, trials did not show clear clinical benefit in CF) and access would require a trial or compassionate-use pathway, with BUB1B-specific readthrough still to be demonstrated.

lever: Read through the premature stop codon
why: An approved topical anti-aphthous-ulcer drug reported to both inhibit nonsense-mediated decay and promote readthrough, potentially raising the pool of BUB1B transcript available for readthrough.
caveat: Systemic exposure and safety for chronic oral use are not established and NMD inhibition is a broad, potentially harmful perturbation, so transcript-level and protein-level rescue in patient fibroblasts would need to be shown before any consideration.

why: Microtubule-destabilising agent that is the backbone of standard rhabdomyosarcoma regimens (with dactinomycin/cyclophosphamide), and a reduced-intensity version of this regimen has been reported in a BUB1B-related MVA patient with rhabdomyosarcoma (PMID 31184400).
caveat: Only relevant if a tumour is actually documented and biopsied; spindle-assembly-checkpoint-deficient cells may respond atypically to antimitotics (slippage vs. hypersensitivity), and constitutional aneuploidy may worsen myelotoxicity and neurotoxicity, so dose tolerance and tumour response would have to be established prospectively.

why: Approved component of VA/VAC rhabdomyosarcoma therapy, giving a conventional, evidence-based option should an RMS arise in this patient.
caveat: Genotoxic mechanism raises theoretical concern about secondary malignancy and organ toxicity in a chromosomally unstable, cancer-predisposed host, so tolerability in MVA would need to be demonstrated case by case.

why: Approved 26S proteasome inhibitor proposed to exploit the proteotoxic/protein-folding stress of aneuploid cells, with prior phase II testing in advanced sarcoma (NCT00027716).
caveat: The aneuploidy-vulnerability rationale is preclinical and untested in MVA-associated tumours, and sarcoma trial activity has been minimal, so tumour-specific sensitivity and paediatric tolerability would both need to be shown.

why: Approved mTOR inhibitor that has been randomised in relapsed/refractory rhabdomyosarcoma in children, offering a non-genotoxic option that may suit a cancer-predisposition background.
caveat: No MVA- or BUB1B-specific data exist, and benefit would need demonstration in the actual tumour, with attention to immunosuppression and metabolic toxicity.

why: Approved MEK inhibitor relevant to fusion-negative rhabdomyosarcoma with RAS-pathway mutations, which can only be assigned after tumour sequencing.
caveat: Entirely contingent on finding an activating RAS/MAPK lesion in a tumour that may never occur, and paediatric cutaneous, ocular and cardiac toxicities require monitoring.

mechanisms: Dual specificity mitogen-activated protein kinase kinase; MEK1/2 inhibitor
